event: VXE 500 (Edge asset, fuel cell, heated pitot prototype) descended extremely slowly in VTOL through freezing fog on landings on 2/3 and 2/4 2025, landing with only 36% battery on 2/3; no damage.
failure_mode: False short range returns from freezing fog (about 5 ft read at about 500 ft AGL) were accepted into the VTOL AGL estimate, so the VTOL AP believed it was near the ground and slowed its descent
contributing: VTOL AGL estimate had no check rejecting unreasonable LRF ranges in VTOL flight (fix proposed in FS2-2852)
Heated pitot corrupting OAT and baro altitude (VXEP-976), possibly the cause of the 2/4 slow descent

evidence.quote: Upon descending into the FZFG the aircraft seemed to slow its decent rate drastically.
The freezing fog environment is apparently one of those conditions, causing the LRF to measure ranges on the order of a 5 ft when its height above ground was around 500 ft.
The simple fix is to exclude unreasonable LRF range measurements from the AGL estimate.
The second landing issue may very well be due to the VTOL altitude though and not FZFG

team_root_cause: Freezing fog impacting laser altimeter measurement causing artificially low readings.

would_settle_it.what: LRF range and AGL estimate during the 2/4 descent, to tell an LRF false return from the heated pitot OAT baro error

reasoning: The crew saw the descent rate collapse on entering freezing fog. The engineer who analysed the data (root cause on VXEP-976) found the LRF reporting about 5 ft at about 500 ft in the fog, and FS2-2852 proposes filtering such readings. That names the LRF and the mechanism for the 2/3 landing; the 2/4 landing may instead be the heated pitot altitude error.
notes: FS2-2851 is a duplicate of this ticket (same text, no comments). Two events on this ticket: 2/3 landing (main) and 2/4 landing, which the operator says may be the separate VTOL altitude issue (VXEP-976, heated pitot OAT). A comment says it was briefly moved to canceled as a known weather limitation.

event: VXE 560 (PMA263) main battery connector was found extremely hot during an on-site SD card rework on FSK ground power, and arced when a main battery was then plugged in; no flight involved.
component: AS150 power contact (anti-spark contact on fuselage power harness 107-102189-1, SN 0141)
failure_mode: Connector not fully engaged, so load current ran through the 6 ohm anti-spark inrush resistor (about 8 to 9 V drop, 8 to 9 W), which overheated and permanently rose to 18 ohm
contributing: Non anti-spark harness pin measured 0.264 in against 0.28 in expected
Harness from an outsourced Compass Systems batch that also includes SN 0157 from the VXEP-999 crash
Battery and FSK power cable used are not identified, so their sockets could not be measured

evidence.quote: Main battery connector anti-spark resistance measured at 18 ohms, 3 times the expected resistance
The test shown no other indication or reason for heating up the power connector than the battery connection was not engaged fully
there is a lower-than-expected voltage reading for apVbatt at around 19V
Harness pin diameters were measured: anti-spark measured at 0.275in and non antispark measured at 0.264in
Anti-Spark should be 0.275in and the non anti-spark should be 0.28.
Electronic Failure - Excessive heat on main battery connector, noted arcing issues. Avionics is not sealed.

team_root_cause: This issue may be caused by inconsistent socket contacts

would_settle_it.what: apVbatt near 19 V while drawing about 1 A, confirming current through the anti-spark resistor

would_settle_it.file: Battery and FSK power cable used at the customer site
would_settle_it.what: Socket diameters of the mating side, to separate an undersized harness pin from an undersized socket

attachments_read: 28296_Amended RMA Repair and Upgrade Quote for VXE-560 Warranty PMA263 250116-3 April 15, 2025.pdf.md
reasoning: The anti-spark contact measured 18 ohm against 6 ohm expected, and the XCOMM log shows apVbatt near 19 V instead of 28 V, which matches current flowing through the inrush resistor. Bench testing found no short and concluded the battery connection was not fully engaged. The harness non anti-spark pin was measured undersized, which with the known AS150 fit problems (VXEP-540) points at the harness connector, though the mating battery and cable were never measured.
notes: Invoice pages 6 to 15 are scans with no text. The harness was replaced under RMA-467.

event: VXE 598 with center wing 596 (PMA263, 29 Palms) lost link and video during a high climb on 30 Jan 2025, regained it briefly during RTB, then lost it again and crashed into terrain.
component: AS150 power contact (main battery sockets and fuselage power harness 107-102189-1 SN 0157 anti-spark contact)
failure_mode: Undersized main battery AS150 sockets (0.272 and 0.273 in) prevented a full mate; high contact resistance degraded under a long high-current climb, causing a brownout and voltage drop that took down the FWAP and link
contributing: Climb of about 4000 ft at 58 A, beyond the manual limit of 2000 ft before a 5 minute break
Harness from the same outsourced Compass Systems batch as VXEP-985
Low main battery cell voltages likely from staying powered for hours after the crash

evidence.quote: The main battery sockets measured 0.273 and 0.272, which are out of spec for the AS150 contacts
AS150 antispark on the Fuse Power harness measuring ~27 ohms (6 ohms expected)
When powering the Avionics, the Fuselage Power Harness was unusually difficult to fully mate, requiring more force than usual
I believe the root cause is due to bad mating on the main battery. This would explain the brown out at the higher altitude and the voltage drop seen in the logs.
Instead, this aircraft pulled 58A during an ascent for 4000 feet.
Cannot confirm it over heated - can only heavily assume, so our description should match as such

team_root_cause: Some evidence of fuse power harness damage due to OOS socket contacts on the battery. @Adrian Garcia please update findings and plan in above and in the ppt. See https://jenaero.atlassian.net/browse/VXEP-540

would_settle_it.what: Battery voltage against current during the climb, showing voltage staying low after current drops (bad connection)
apVbatt and apIbatt through the climb and the FWAP reset time
Final investigation conclusions and the FW ESC and FWAP inspection results

reasoning: The main battery sockets measured below the 0.275 in AS150 spec, the harness was very hard to mate, and its anti-spark contact read about 27 ohm against 6 ohm expected, all direct measurements on this aircraft. VXEP-540 shows sockets at 0.273 in or less cause incomplete mates and a voltage drop, and the logs show a voltage drop consistent with a brownout. The team agrees but notes overheating is assumed, and a later review blamed a hard climb and possibly the FW ESC circuit, so one alternative remains.
notes: Customer report says center wing 597; ticket and RMA say 596. Customer report differs from the first email (commanded -900 AGL). RMA-528 later called it operator error for warranty, after Samuel Lopez noted the 58 A, 4000 ft climb and suspected the FWD ESC circuit for the FWAP shutdown. The as150 profile report attachment is only a vendor brochure. RMA-528 PDFs 02182025 and Intake are scans with no text. RMA-529 (camera RMA) not read.

event: On Edge asset VXE 734 on 14 Feb 2025, a student found the gimbal mounting plate warm and arcing to the fuselage on the ground.
component: E140Z G2 gimbal (SN EPS 6182) ground tied to housing, with conductive mount plate MP-0067-063-01
failure_mode: Ground loop: gimbal power and signal grounds tied to its chassis, conducted through the metal mount and plate into the fuselage and back through the Silvus radio body, carrying current that heated and arced at the plate
contributing: Conductive aluminum mount and painted metal plate in use instead of non-conductive parts
Silvus enclosure power return common with its case, giving a return path through the fuselage

evidence.quote: While investigating VXEP-813, I discovered 3.5 to 4 Ohms between ground pins (J2.1 and J2.9) to gimbal base.
the other multimeter pin on the rear screw hole of the Silvus and we got a reading of 5 ohms
The mount and plate from the incident were conductive.
Power on after BIT: (meter and probes configured for DC current): Reading ~32 mA flowing from Gimbal to plane
Confirmed gimbal GND is tied to housing

team_root_cause: 5 May 25: The root cause appears to be a ground loop facilitated by the gimbal having internal power and signal grounds tied to the chassis COMBINED with a path to ground on VXE30 through the fuselage and the Silvus.
reasoning: Resistance measurements show the gimbal ground pins tied to the gimbal base (3.5 to 4 ohm) and the aircraft power assembly tied to the Silvus body (5 ohm). The incident mount and plate were conductive, and earlier tests on the same aircraft measured about 32 mA flowing from gimbal to airframe. Tests with non-conductive mounts showed no fault, so the ground loop through the conductive mount is directly supported.
notes: Early comments conflicted on whether the incident mount was conductive; the reporter later confirmed the incident mount and plate were conductive. Corrective action subtasks VXEP-1037 and VXEP-1038 were canceled as Won't Do.

event: USASOC VXE 548 (5th Group, OCONUS) showed COMMAND_AUXSERVO failed warnings at the surface check step of the launch wizard on two GCSs; the aircraft was held from flight and no damage occurred.
component: GCS mission simulation (blocking, run on the launch wizard Mission Checkout page)
failure_mode: A long mission simulation froze the GCS for about 50 seconds, stopping uplink so the FWAP flagged a GCS link timeout; afterwards the servo center (31) and disarm (32) system commands failed, shown by the GCS as COMMAND_AUXSERVO
contributing: Fixed wing AP on outdated firmware 6.05o (6.2 release) while the rest ran 6.3
Large complex mission from a previous customer loaded on the GCS
GCS does not retry or check link health before sending system commands

evidence.quote: Fault value of 0x0005C000 with bit mask of #define VT_FAULT_LINK_APRX 0x00040000 is 1 indicating a fault with the aprx link.
In the GCS log (_171620_log.csv) There is a 51 second gap in log records right before the incident.
I was able to recreate the link outage, with a long mission sim time, but not the failed system commands.
The customer tried a default mission, and the syscmd failures did not occur.
GCS Mission Simulation blocks the GCS from sending any messages to the vehicle which can create a vehicle connection timeout after 50 seconds.
They are running 6.05o (6.2 release) and the rest of the software (GCS, XComm, VTOL) is from release 6.3.

team_root_cause: Issue appears to be caused by long mission simulations which lead to uplink outage and instability. With a default mission the issue did not occur, however, no further tests were completed to attempt recreating the issue.

would_settle_it.what: Repeat of the failure with the original long mission reloaded, to confirm the sim causes the system command failures

reasoning: XCOMM logged the FWAP uplink fault just before the failed commands, the GCS log has a 51 second gap while a mission simulation ran, and engineering reproduced the link outage with a long mission sim. A short default mission and a firmware update stopped the warnings. The failed commands themselves were not reproduced, so the cause is narrowed to the blocking GCS mission simulation with medium confidence.
notes: VXEP-600 showed link drops before the surface check page reproduce the same servo center and disarm failures. No FDR was in the AAR packages.
